report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. text.text: Polarization can be described as when opinions and attitudes discontinue existing on a continuum and are drawn to opposing extremes.

Affective polarization refers to the positive feelings and associations towards one's own political ingroup, in combination with negative feelings and associations that arise towards the outgroup on the other end of the spectrum.
Recent studies have shown that polarization is increasing in several countries.
This change is happening simultaneously with increases in singleness and loneliness.
Moreover, a historically significant political gap can be observed in many Western countries between young men and women, raising questions regarding heterosexual relationship formation.

The current study set out to examine differences in affective polarization in men and women, and to test loneliness, age, and relationship status as predictors of affective polarization in a Nordic multiparty democracy.
We used a population-based sample of 7,357 Finnish adults who responded to an online survey.
In line with previous findings, men were found more likely to be TAN (traditional-authoritariannationalist)-polarized, and women more likely to be GAL (green-alternative-libertarian)polarized.
In addition, polarization was found to be more common among younger respondents.
Surprisingly, relationship status was not found to be a significant predictor of affective polarization.
Loneliness was found to be more common in GAL-, but not in TANpolarized respondents, indicating that less moderate political alignment may be associated with loneliness in general.
The present study examined affective polarization, the gender political gap, and associations with pair bonds and loneliness in a Finnish population-based sample collected in 2022.

Previous research indicates that political polarization has significantly increased in several countries, and that affective polarization has increased in some regions but not in others (Boxell et al., 2021; Emanuele & Marino, 2024; Garzia et al., 2023; Geiger, 2014; Brenan, 2025).

text.text: Previous research has shown that individuals have a consistent proclivity to perceive the ingroup more positively than the out-group; a phenomenon called intergroup bias (Hewstone et al., 2024).

text.text: This phenomenon is in accordance with the typical self-serving attributional bias, that is, the proclivity to interpret successes as due to one's own performance, but failures as due to external factors (Gioia & Sims Jr., 1985).

text.text: This bias is ubiquitous in intergroup relations, and an individual's favorable social identity can be built on comparisons between the own in-group, and certain outgroups, where the purpose is to highlight one's own group as positively distinct, as compared to others (Hewstone et al., 2024; Tajfel & Turner, 2004).

text.text: The political sphere is no exception to intergroup bias.

It has been shown that intergroup bias is common among voters, and that partisan identity can motivate affective polarization (Sheffer, 2020). text.text: Studies on group biases and group effects have shed light on how affective polarization functions.

When studying affective polarization, it is not merely the positive feelings and associations towards the in-group which are measured, but also the negative feelings and associations towards the out-group.

Research on intergroup bias has highlighted the importance of considering the attitudes towards the outgroup; Negational categorization (i.e. defining one's identity by what one is not rather than what one is) affects and shapes one's own social identity and can increase outgroup derogation (Zhong et al., 2008).

text.text: Therefore, studying polarization not only in terms of individuals' own political value orientations, but also in terms of negative evaluations and affect toward others', becomes increasingly relevant.
An individual's own political value orientation can be defined as the person's beliefs on how society should function and be structured.

A two-dimensional model is often used to visualize individuals' political value orientation, where one dimension describes ideological differences in the role of economic redistribution and state intervention on a left-right axis.

The other dimension is cultural and non-economic, and has been described through different concept pairings, such as libertarianism vs authoritarianism; liberalism vs conservatism; and post-materialism vs materialism.
The group of these three concept pairings has been labeled as GAL-TAN, that is, green-alternativelibertarian vs traditional-authoritarian-nationalist (Söderlund, 2023).
In contemporary Western Europe, GAL-views tend to be consolidated with the economic left, and TAN-views tend to be consolidated with the economic right (Brigevich et al. 2019).
text.formatted: In contemporary Western Europe, GAL-views tend to be consolidated with the economic left, and TAN-views tend to be consolidated with the economic right <ref type="bibr">(Brigevich et al. 2019)</ref>.

text.text: This is crucial to point out, as much of the research on political views has used the left-right axis for measuring political differences.

Although the present study uses the two-dimensional GAL-TAN model, it is worth noting that research shows that the GAL/TAN-categorization is not entirely dichotomous, and that parties can simultaneously have some values from one category and other values from another (Brigevich et al., 2017).

text.text: Research on the relationship between political leanings and loneliness is limited.
Current findings pertaining to politics seem to suggest that loneliness is both associated with supporting a radical or populist political party and with political disengagement.

A study by Langenkamp and Bienstman (2022) found an association between weak social belonging and voting for populist parties on the right, but the association between social belonging and support for left-wing populist parties was weak and inconsistent. Peterson et al. (2025) studied the association between loneliness and support for the radical right, finding a statistically significant association between the two.

text.text: Whilst a connection between populist support and loneliness appears to be emerging in the evidence, loneliness is also tied to being politically disengaged.

Lonely individuals are less likely to vote in elections and experience a lower sense of voting duty (Langenkamp, 2021), also believing that they have a low influence on politics (Langenkamp & Stepanova, 2024).

text.text: In sum, it appears that lonely individuals are more likely than non-lonely individuals to both show political disengagement and support for populist or more radical parties.

text.text: It is still unclear how affective polarization could potentially affect loneliness and relationship status.
The current study set out to explore these phenomena in a multi-party democracy with moderate levels of affective polarization.

This study is the first, to the best of my knowledge, to examine the association between relationship status and affective polarization, and the first Finnish study to examine the association between affective polarization and loneliness.

Based on previous findings, I postulated the following hypotheses: (1) Men will be more likely to feel warmth towards parties with TAN-values, while simultaneously having negative feelings towards parties with GAL-values (i.e., to be TAN-polarized).

Women will be more likely to feel warmth towards parties with GAL-values, while simultaneously having negative feeling towards parties with TAN-values (i.e., be GAL-polarized); (2) Younger respondents will be more likely to be affectively polarized; (3) Singleness will be more common in polarized respondents than in non-polarized respondents; and (4) Loneliness will be more common in polarized respondents than in not polarized.
The data used in the present study stemmed from a large, population-based sample of Finnish twins, as well as siblings and parents of twins.
Twin families and their postal addresses were obtained from the Digital and Population Data Services Agency of Finland, which maintains the national population registry.
In total, addresses to 50,771 individuals were obtained from the registry in the summer of 2021.
Over the period from October 2021 to February 2022, these individuals were sent an invitation letter by postal mail to participate in an anonymous online survey.

Each individual was assigned a randomly generated, eight-character personal code, which they could use to log on to the survey (these randomly generated codes were subsequently used to match individuals belonging to the same family, however, so that personal information and survey responses were never combined or stored together).
Individuals who did not respond in any way were sent a reminder letter 2-3 weeks after the arrival of the first invitation letter.

In order to incentivize participation, invitees were offered the possibility to participate in a raffle for 100 gift cards worth €25 apiece to S-Ryhmä, a business conglomerate operating, for example, shops, grocery stores, hotels, restaurants and petrol stations across Finland (an individual could only win one gift card).
In total, 12,269 individuals responded (24%) and of these, 854 individuals declined to give informed consent, leaving us with responses from 11,415 individuals.
It should be noted, however, that this response rate likely represents an underestimate.
For example, according to national statistics, up to 10% of Finns move each year (https://www.stat.fi/).
text.formatted: For example, according to national statistics, up to 10% of Finns move each year (<ref type="url" target="https://www.stat.fi/">https://www.stat.fi/</ref>).

text.text: We do not know how many of the potential participants we failed to reach (e.g., due to changing addresses or death) between when the addresses were obtained from the population registry and when the invitation letters were sent out.

The final sample for the current study was 7,357 respondents, after selecting one participant per family to eliminate confounding effects of familial resemblance and excluding two participants due to them reporting simultaneous GAL-and TAN-polarization in their responses.
The survey collected demographic information on the participants.
This information included age, level of education, current socioeconomic status and relationship status.

Relationship status was assessed with the question: "Are you in a romantic or sexual relationship with someone at the moment?", with the response options being "no relationship", "I have a sexual partner, but I'm not in a relationship" or "Yes, I am in a romantic relationship".
Participants who reported being in a romantic relationship were categorized as such, participants who selected one of the remaining two responses were categorized as single.
Information about the gender of participants was obtained from the Central Population Registry (legally registered as male or female).
Loneliness was measured with the UCLA-3-item-loneliness scale, which has been shown to measure loneliness with adequate reliability and validity (Hughes et al., 2004).

The answers were recoded to a Likert scale of 1-11.
Three groups were then identified for the statistical analyses.

The GAL-polarized group included respondents who had rated the Left Alliance and/or the Green Party very affirmatively (10 or 11 points on the 11-point scale) while also giving a very negative rating (1 or 2 points on the 11-point scale) to the Finns Party or the Christian Democrats.

The TAN-polarized group included respondents with the inverse scores to the aforementioned group (i.e., very negative ratings to the Left Alliance and the Green Party, and very affirmative ratings to the Finns Party and the Christian Democrats).
The control group in the study consisted of non-polarized respondents, that is, respondents who did not meet criteria for neither GAL-nor TAN-polarization.

A multinomial logistic regression model was used to test all four of the hypotheses of the present study.
The dependent variable in the regression model was affective polarization, while the four independent variables were gender, age, relationship status and loneliness.
There were a total of 431 GAL-polarized respondents in the sample, and a total of 173 TANpolarized respondents in the sample.

Out of the 6,753 individuals who had responded to the questions regarding the political parties, the distribution was as follows: 100 men were 16 GAL-polarized, 100 men were TAN-polarized, 331 women were GAL-polarized, and 73 women were TAN-polarized.

The present study aimed to explore affective polarization in Finland and its associations with gender, age, relationship status and loneliness.

This question was of particular interest due to reports of increases in polarization and a gender gap in politics, especially among young adults, simultaneously to a decrease in the proportion of the population who are in committed romantic relationships, especially among young adults.
The first hypothesis, proposing that men will be more likely to be TAN-polarized, while women will be more likely to be GAL-polarized, was supported with a moderate effect size.
The second hypothesis, proposing that young respondents will be more likely to be affectively polarized was also supported: younger participants were more likely to be both GALand TAN-polarized.

The third hypothesis, that being single will be more common in polarized respondents was surprisingly not confirmed -no significant relationship was found between affective polarization and relationship status.

The fourth hypothesis, positing that loneliness will be more common in polarized respondents was partially supported; a relationship was found between loneliness and being GAL-polarized, but not being TAN-polarized.

As predicted, a gender gap was found in our sample; Men were more likely TAN-polarized and women were more likely GAL-polarized, and this finding is in line with previous research (Burn-Murdoch, 2024; Saad et al., 2024).

text.text: Considering that the tendency for women to vote more conservatively and religiously than men has been observed in several Western countries historically, with men notably identifying themselves as more left-leaning than women until the 1980s (Duverger, 1955; Norris, 1999; Oskarson & Ahlbom, 2021), these results indicate a historically relevant shift in the political sphere.

text.text: Regarding the results of the current study, it is worth noting that the sample consisted of equally many TAN-and GAL-polarized men, meaning that men in our sample were equally likely to be polarized on both ends of the spectrum.

As Finnish men vote for the selected TAN-parties combined at higher rates than the selected GAL-parties combined (Paloheimo 2024; Suuronen et al., 2020; Yle, 2022), this result could indicate a potential sampling bias.

text.text: This sampling bias is unlikely to have over-exaggerated the gender gap, rather it may have potentially underestimated it.
Several factors have been suggested to explain the gender gap.
Women's religiosity has decreased (Shorrocks 2018), and fewer gender gaps have been observed in religious societies (Langsæther and Knutsen, 2025).

text.text: Another potential explanatory factor is women's increased participation in waged labor, as women's work participation is associated with women being more left-leaning (De Vaus & McAllister, 1989).

text.text: Women having become more liberal and left is a consistent finding in recent decades, while men on the other hand, in part have also become more liberal, and in part have become more right-wing.
It seems to be both policy questions and voters' identity which can affect their voting choices.
There are certain policy questions which appear to differ more strongly between men and women;

Henriksson (2023) finds the largest differences in questions regarding sexual and gender minorities, but also questions regarding public service cuts and climate action show some differences between the genders.
Nevertheless, research on social sorting has found that affective polarization can be driven by social identity and party identity aligning, irrespective of policy questions.
Through the process of social sorting, social identity can become increasingly linked with a party, and this has been found to drive strong emotions to all threats and reassurances (Mason, 2016).

text.text: Therefore, while women and men have differing opinions on certain policy questions, affective polarization can further be strengthened by social and party identity, even when opinions do not differ (Mason, 2016).

text.text: In the current study, no association was found between being single and being affectively polarized.

As previous research has indicated that political values can affect partner choice, how attractive one is perceived as, and one's dating prospects (Bagel, 2024; Huber & Malhotra, 2017; Indikator Opinion, 2025; Nicholson et al., 2016), and that dissimilar political affiliation in a romantic relationship is less common (Gordon et al., 2024), it would seem plausible that heterosexual romantic relationship formation could be affected by affective polarization and the political gender gap.

text.text: Although the current study affirmed the gender gap, the third hypothesis, that singleness and affective polarization would be related, was not confirmed.
To the best of my knowledge, no prior research has investigated whether there is an association between relationship status and affective polarization, making the present study the first to do so.
Several perspectives could be taken into account to potentially explain the unpredicted result.

As the gender gap and singleness appear to be more common among youth, and failing to account for cohort differences can underestimate gender differences (Rauer et al., 2013; Shorrocks, 2018; United States Census Bureau, 2023), I decided to replicate the analysis but only with participants below the age of 30.

text.text: No association between relationship status and affective polarization was found in this additional analysis either, disproving the hypothesis that generational differences would have been the cause for the unconfirmed third hypothesis.
An alternative explanation could be party dislike not transferring strongly to voter dislike.

In a 2023 study, Strandberg asked Finns how willing they would be to be friends with a supporter of a certain party, finding that Finns were relatively willing to be friends with a supporter of another party.
Most people had only one party whose supporters they were most unwilling to be friends with.

The fact that the strength of party dislike did not directly translate into the same level of strong unwillingness to be friends with a party supporter, could indicate that the polarization between political parties is stronger than the hostility between individuals supporting those parties.

Potential difficulties in finding a romantic partner due to political views could also be mediated by dating prospects within the same cluster, or in dating the supporters of a party which is least disliked in the opposing cluster.
A multi-party political system might have a protective effect against involuntary singleness caused by difficulty in finding a romantic partner with shared political views.

In order to achieve power in a multi-party system, governments have to be formed of parties with somewhat different ideologies collaborating, potentially strengthening sympathy to voters in the same cluster, rather than only the same party.

Thus, considering that affective polarization may look different depending on the specific country and political system, studying of the third hypothesis in a different context, particularly one with a two-party system, could be of interest.
A relevant perspective to be taken into consideration is the previously mentioned potential sampling bias in the current study.

National polls from the same time period as when invitations to the survey used in the present study were sent out, show approval ratings that are dissimilar from the views reported in the present study (Orjala, 2022).

text.text: National polls consistently show respondents having higher or similar levels of support for the selected TAN-parties collectively, than the selected GAL-parties collectively (Paloheimo, 2024; Suuronen et al., 2020; Orjala, 2022).

text.text: In our data, respondents reported more positive views towards the selected GAL-parties than towards the selected TAN-parties, indicating some sampling bias.
It seems that TAN-polarized individuals were underrepresented in our data, resulting in a potential sampling bias affecting the outcomes of the analyses.

It is therefore possible that affective polarization could have a true association with relationship status, especially if the effect size is small and TAN-rather than GAL-polarization is the driver of this hypothesized association.
If this was the case, it could come to light in future research using a more representative sample.
It is also worth noting that singleness is increasingly common in the modern day.
A notable proportion of singles are not looking for a romantic partner, and many are reporting that being single is according to their liking (Brown, 2020; Lei & South, 2021).

Furthermore, as relationship status at a given point is a limited measure of romantic relationships, future research could expand the understanding of affective polarization in relation to romantic relationships by studying features such as relationship quality or duration.
In the present study, GAL-polarization was significantly associated with higher levels of loneliness, but TAN-polarization was not.

Previous research on political leanings and loneliness is limited, however some studies have found an association between loneliness and support for populist parties and the radical right (Langenkamp & Bienstman, 2022; Peterson et al. 2025).

text.text: The results of the current study present evidence for an association between loneliness and support for left-wing parties.

A previous study showed that rejection-sensitive individuals who are rejected are more apt to identify with and support a radical group (Renström et al., 2020), providing a hypothesis for the association between loneliness and more radical political support.

text.text: The results of the current study strengthen the hypothesis for an association between loneliness and affective polarization or support for less moderate parties generally.
The results highlight that loneliness may also be more common among GAL-polarized individuals.

A general tendency for polarized individuals and those supporting less moderate parties to be lonelier would explain why the GAL-polarized individuals in the current study were more likely to report higher degrees of loneliness, but not why the TAN-polarized were not lonelier than non-polarized individuals.
The previously mentioned sampling bias may have affected the results, as the TANpolarized individuals were underrepresented.
Furthermore, it is worth mentioning that most of the parties selected for the current study are parties with a fair amount of support.
The party with the least support of the ones selected was a religious center-right party, which previous research focusing on populist or radical right support could be less applicable to.

In general, it is worth noting that the Finnish political field is considered to have low levels of ideological polarization, low levels of conflict, and to be consensus-driven (Kawecki, 2022; Kekkonen & Ylä-Anttila, 2021).

text.text: Women were overrepresented in the sample of the current study (64.8%), and as mentioned above, it seems that some groups of participants (particularly TAN-polarized men) were underrepresented, potentially skewing the results.
In the present study, respondents indicated how warmly (affirmatively) or coldly (negatively) they feel towards the most common Finnish parties, but these feelings were not further explored.

For future research, it would be of interest to study to which degree these feelings translate to the level of animosity or friendliness towards the voters of other political parties in a multi-party system, as previous research has shown that party dislike does not translate into voter dislike at the same strength (Strandberg, 2023).

text.text: Future research is still needed to determine whether being affectively polarized plays a role in relationship formation.
Relationship status at a given point in time is a limited measure of one's romantic experience.

Future research could expand the understanding of the relationship between affective polarization and romantic relationships through studying other aspects of romantic relationships, such as relationship quality in current or previous relationships, and individuals' own evaluations of their relationship status and dating prospects.

Future research could explore whether affectively polarized individuals are more likely to remain single, and whether they, once partnered, have higher levels of conflict, and whether being affectively polarized is associated with an increased or decreased likelihood of romantic relationships ending.

Furthermore, it could be of interest for future research to investigate whether the relationship between affective polarization and romantic relationships differs in a two-party political system, in contrast to the multi-party system of the current study.

A relevant question for future research is how strongly affective polarization between political parties transfers to hostility, conflict or negative consequences in romantic and platonic relationships, and daily social interactions.

Considering that some studies have found younger adults to be more polarized than older adults (Shorrocks, 2018; United States Census Bureau, 2023), future research could take this into consideration by studying age cohorts separately.

The current Finnish parliamentary parties are as follows; the National Coalition Party, a center-right party valuing individual freedom, market economy and competition; the Finnish Social Democratic Party, a center-left party valuing social security and the rights of workers; the Centre Party of Finland, a centrist party valuing agriculture and quality of life in rural areas; the Finns Party, a right-wing party valuing nationalism and conservative values; the Greens, a center-left green party valuing social justice and protecting the environment; the Left Alliance, a leftwing party valuing social justice and social security; Swedish People's Party of Finland, a liberal center-right party valuing the interests of the Swedish-speaking population and entrepreneurship; Christian Democrats in Finland, a center-right party valuing Christian and conservative principles; and Movement Now, a center-right party with only one MP (The Finnish Parliament, 2025; PolitPro, 2025; Europe Elects, 2025).
Affective polarization has been studied in Finland by Strandberg (2023), who found that Finnish voters could be divided into clusters based on how much they liked other parties.
One cluster was formed by the Left Alliance, the Social Democratic Party and the Green League, who viewed each other positively.
The opposite cluster consisted of the Centre Party, the Finns Party, Movement Now, and the Christian Democrats.
The least liked parties were the Left Alliance, Movement Now and the Finns Party.
